claim: Tarantula toxins that bind to voltage-sensing domains of voltage-activated ion channels are thought to partition into the membrane and bind to the channel within the bilayer.
source: Tarantula toxins that bind to voltage-sensing domains of voltage-activated ion channels are thought to partition into the membrane and bind to the channel within the bilayer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this model.

claim: Psalmotoxin (PcTx1) was recently crystallized in complex with the extracellular domain of an acid sensing ion channel (ASIC).
source: While no structures of a voltage-sensor toxin bound to a channel have been solved, a structural homolog, psalmotoxin (PcTx1), was recently crystalized in complex with the extracellular domain of an acid sensing ion channel (ASIC).
evidence: This is a factual statement about a structural determination, supported by the existence of crystal structures.

claim: Both voltage-sensor toxins and PcTx1 interact with membranes.
source: Our results show that both types of tarantula toxins interact with membranes, but that voltage-sensor toxins partition deeper into the bilayer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Voltage-sensor toxins partition deeper into the bilayer than PcTx1.
source: Our results show that both types of tarantula toxins interact with membranes, but that voltage-sensor toxins partition deeper into the bilayer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brominated lipid quenching experiments (Figure 3E, F).

claim: Tarantula toxins have evolved a similar concave surface for clamping onto α-helices that is effective in aqueous or lipidic physical environments.
source: In addition, our results suggest that tarantula toxins have evolved a similar concave surface for clamping onto α-helices that is effective in aqueous or lipidic physical environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data and structural comparisons (Figure 5).

claim: Scorpion toxins that physically block the pore of K+ channels were initially used to identify pore-forming regions of the channel.
source: For example, scorpion toxins that physically block the pore of K+ channels (MacKinnon and Miller, 1988) were initially used to identify pore-forming regions of the channel (MacKinnon and Miller, 1989), and to determine the stoichiometry of subunits (MacKinnon, 1991), inactivation gates (MacKinnon et al., 1993), as well as accessory subunits (Morin and Kobertz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tarantula and scorpion toxins can bind to voltage-sensing domains in voltage-activated ion channels and either retard or facilitate activation in response to changes in voltage.
source: For example, both tarantula and scorpion toxins can bind to voltage-sensing domains in voltage-activated ion channels and either retard or facilitate activation in response to changes in voltage (Rogers et al., 1996; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997a, 1997b; Cestèle et al., 1998; Milescu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Voltage-sensor toxins have been valuable tools to explore the mechanism of voltage sensing.
source: This second class of toxins have been valuable tools to explore the mechanism of voltage sensing (Phillips et al., 2005; Alabi et al., 2007; Campos et al., 2007, 2008) and the roles of individual voltage sensors in the mechanisms of activation and inactivation (Campos et al., 2007; Bosmans et al., 2008; Campos et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tarantula toxins have been discovered that activate transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
source: Tarantula toxins have also been discovered that activate transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Bohlen et al., 2010), and both tarantula toxin and snake toxins have been identified that activate acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) (Chen et al., 2006; Salinas et al., 2006; Bohlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tarantula toxins and snake toxins have been identified that activate acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC).
source: Tarantula toxins have also been discovered that activate transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Bohlen et al., 2010), and both tarantula toxin and snake toxins have been identified that activate acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) (Chen et al., 2006; Salinas et al., 2006; Bohlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxins were used to stabilize specific conformations of TRPV1 channel and ASICs for structure determination by cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction.
source: For both the TRPV1 channel and ASICs, these toxins were used to stabilize specific conformations for structure determination by cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012; Baconguis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Hanatoxin and GxTx-1E are thought to target voltage-activated potassium (Kv) channels by partitioning into the lipid membrane and binding to their voltage-sensing domains.
source: Tarantula toxins such as hanatoxin and GxTx-1E are thought to target voltage-activated potassium (Kv) channels by partitioning into the lipid membrane and binding to their voltage-sensing domains to modify how the channel opens in response to changes in membrane voltage (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997a, 1997b; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 2000, 2001; Lee and MacKinnon, 2004; Wang et al., 2004; Phillips et al., 2005; Alabi et al., 2007; Milescu et al., 2007, 2009, 2013; Schmidt and MacKinnon, 2008; Bosmans et al., 2011a; Tilley et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous work.

claim: The strong interaction of tarantula toxins with lipid membranes is mediated by a prominent amphipathic surface on the toxins.
source: The strong interaction of these tarantula toxins with lipid membranes is mediated by a prominent amphipathic surface on the toxins (Figure 1F) (Takahashi et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2004, 2010), which facilitates their entry into the membrane (Lee and MacKinnon, 2004; Milescu et al., 2007, 2009; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1F showing the amphipathic surface.

claim: No structures of complexes between tarantula toxins and Kv channels have been solved.
source: Although many aspects of this inhibitory mechanism have been well-studied (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997a, 1997b; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998, 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2004; Phillips et al., 2005; Alabi et al., 2007; Milescu et al., 2007, 2009; Bosmans et al., 2011a; Milescu et al., 2013; Mihailescu et al., 2014; Tilley et al., 2014), no structures of complexes between tarantula toxins and Kv channels have been solved, limiting our understanding of how tarantula toxins dock onto voltage sensors and influence their conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of structural data, supported by the lack of such structures in the literature.

claim: PcTx1 was recently crystallized in complex with ASIC1a.
source: However, a structurally related tarantula toxin named PcTx1 was recently crystalized in complex with ASIC1a (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012) (Figure 1A, left), revealing that the toxin clamps onto the thumb helix-5 (Figure 1G) and inserts an Arginine finger into the subunit interface to interact with residues involved in proton activation of the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and reference to Figure 1A and 1G.

claim: PcTx1 clamps onto the thumb helix-5 of ASIC1a.
source: However, a structurally related tarantula toxin named PcTx1 was recently crystalized in complex with ASIC1a (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012) (Figure 1A, left), revealing that the toxin clamps onto the thumb helix-5 (Figure 1G) and inserts an Arginine finger into the subunit interface to interact with residues involved in proton activation of the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and reference to Figure 1G.

claim: PcTx1 inserts an Arginine finger into the subunit interface to interact with residues involved in proton activation of ASIC1a.
source: However, a structurally related tarantula toxin named PcTx1 was recently crystalized in complex with ASIC1a (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012) (Figure 1A, left), revealing that the toxin clamps onto the thumb helix-5 (Figure 1G) and inserts an Arginine finger into the subunit interface to interact with residues involved in proton activation of the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: PcTx1 modulates the gating properties of ASIC1 channels by enhancing the apparent affinity of these channels for protons.
source: PcTx1 modulates the gating properties of ASIC1 channels by enhancing the apparent affinity of these channels for protons, thereby promoting open and desensitized states of the channel (Escoubas et al., 2000, 2003; Chen et al., 2005; Salinas et al., 2006; Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012), an allosteric mechanism related to that employed by tarantula toxins targeting Kv channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structures of PcTx1 bound to ASIC show that the toxin binds to the protein in aqueous solution far from the transmembrane domains of the channel.
source: However, in contrast to the present model for tarantula toxins binding to Kv channels within the membrane (Figure 1A, right), the structures of PcTx1 bound to ASIC show that the toxin binds to the protein in aqueous solution far from the transmembrane domains of the channel (Figure 1A left).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the binding location.

claim: The overall fold of PcTx1 and voltage sensor toxins are quite similar.
source: Interestingly, the overall fold of PcTx1 and voltage sensor toxins are quite similar (Figure 1H) and PcTx1 has significant amphipathic character (Figure 1D), similar to that seen in the structure of voltage-sensor toxins (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1H showing structural similarity.

claim: PcTx1 has significant amphipathic character similar to that seen in voltage-sensor toxins.
source: Interestingly, the overall fold of PcTx1 and voltage sensor toxins are quite similar (Figure 1H) and PcTx1 has significant amphipathic character (Figure 1D), similar to that seen in the structure of voltage-sensor toxins (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figures 1D and 1E showing amphipathic surfaces.

claim: PcTx1 and GxTx-1E have a similar spacing of six Cys residues that participate in forming disulfide bonds.
source: Both toxins have a similar spacing of six Cys residues that participate in forming disulfide bonds (Figure 1B), and NMR solution structures reveal they adopt similar folds (Figure 1C,D,H), with backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) over 20–22 core residues of 1.0–1.2 Å and over all residues of 2.9 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and structural analysis.

claim: NMR solution structures reveal PcTx1 and GxTx-1E adopt similar folds with backbone RMSD over 20-22 core residues of 1.0-1.2 Å and over all residues of 2.9 Å.
source: Both toxins have a similar spacing of six Cys residues that participate in forming disulfide bonds (Figure 1B), and NMR solution structures reveal they adopt similar folds (Figure 1C,D,H), with backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) over 20–22 core residues of 1.0–1.2 Å and over all residues of 2.9 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and reference to Figures 1C, D, H.

claim: PcTx1 and GxTx-1E have five other positions that are well-conserved, but otherwise their primary sequences vary considerably.
source: The two toxins have five other positions that are well-conserved, but otherwise their primary sequences vary considerably (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PcTx1 contains two solvent-exposed Trp residues, one in loop 1 and one in loop 4.
source: PcTx1 contains two solvent-exposed Trp residues, one in loop 1 and one in loop 4, whereas GxTx-1E contains three, two in loop 1 and one in loop 4.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the toxin structures.

claim: GxTx-1E contains three solvent-exposed Trp residues, two in loop 1 and one in loop 4.
source: PcTx1 contains two solvent-exposed Trp residues, one in loop 1 and one in loop 4, whereas GxTx-1E contains three, two in loop 1 and one in loop 4.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the toxin structures.

claim: The clusters of solvent-exposed hydrophobic residues are on distinct surfaces of PcTx1 and GxTx-1E.
source: The amphipathic character of these toxins can be seen in surface renderings of the toxin structures when coloring residues using the Hessa-Heijne hydrophobicity scale (Hessa et al., 2005), although it is interesting that the clusters of solvent-exposed hydrophobic residues are on distinct surfaces of the two toxins (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figures 1D and 1E showing different hydrophobic surfaces.

claim: Tarantula toxins targeting ion channel voltage sensors interact favorably with lipid membranes.
source: Previous studies have established that tarantula toxins targeting ion channel voltage sensors interact favorably with lipid membranes (Lee and MacKinnon, 2004; Suchyna et al., 2004; Jung et al., 2005; Phillips et al., 2005; Milescu et al., 2007, 2009; Swartz, 2007; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pronounced blue shifts in Trp fluorescence are observed with GxTx-1E when lipid vesicles containing a 1:1 mix of POPC and POPG are added to aqueous solutions of the toxin.
source: Pronounced blue shifts in Trp fluorescence are observed with GxTx-1E when lipid vesicles containing a 1:1 mix of POPC and POPG are added to aqueous solutions of the toxin (Figure 2A), consistent with a previous study (Milescu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GxTx-1E has a mole fraction Kx of 4.6 ± 0.8 × 10^6 for membrane partitioning.
source: Plotting of fluorescence intensity of GxTx-1E in the blue shifted region (320 nm) of the emission spectra as a function of lipid concentration and fitting of a partition function (Figure 2C) yields a mole fraction Kx of 4.6 ± 0.8 × 106, indicating favorable interactions of the toxin with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PcTx1 exhibits detectable blue shifts in emission spectra upon addition of lipid vesicles.
source: To investigate whether PcTx1 can interact with membranes, we performed similar experiments and observed detectable blue shifts in the emission spectra of the toxin upon the addition of lipid vesicles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The blue shifts for PcTx1 were very small (maximal shift of ∼ 2 nm).
source: The blue shifts in the case of PcTx1 were very small (maximal shift of ∼ 2 nm), however, they varied as a function of lipid concentration and saturated at high lipid concentrations, suggestive of an interaction between PcTx1 and lipid membranes.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: The blue shifts for PcTx1 varied as a function of lipid concentration and saturated at high lipid concentrations, suggestive of an interaction between PcTx1 and lipid membranes.
source: The blue shifts in the case of PcTx1 were very small (maximal shift of ∼ 2 nm), however, they varied as a function of lipid concentration and saturated at high lipid concentrations, suggestive of an interaction between PcTx1 and lipid membranes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects.

claim: Lipid vesicles decrease the Stern-Volmer constant for acrylamide quenching of GxTx-1E from 37.7 M^-1 to 9.1 M^-1.
source: In the case of GxTx-1E in aqueous solution, we observed that the Trp fluorescence of the toxin is quenched by the addition of acrylamide in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2E), and fitting of the quenching relationship with a linear function yields a slope (Stern–Volmer constant; Ksv) of 37.7 M−1. Addition of lipid vesicles decreased the Ksv to 9.1 M−1 (Figure 2E), indicating that membranes can shield the Trp residues in GxTx-1E from the soluble quencher.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Membranes can shield the Trp residues in GxTx-1E from the soluble quencher acrylamide.
source: Addition of lipid vesicles decreased the Ksv to 9.1 M−1 (Figure 2E), indicating that membranes can shield the Trp residues in GxTx-1E from the soluble quencher.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the acrylamide quenching data.

claim: PcTx1 exhibits strong quenching by acrylamide in aqueous solution with a Ksv of 29.2 M^-1.
source: When these experiments were performed with PcTx1, we again observed strong quenching by acrylamide in aqueous solution (Ksv of 29.2 M−1) and robust protection of quenching by the addition of lipid vesicles (Ksv of 11.2 M−1; Figure 2F), confirming that PcTx1 can interact with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Addition of lipid vesicles provides robust protection of PcTx1 from acrylamide quenching, reducing Ksv to 11.2 M^-1.
source: When these experiments were performed with PcTx1, we again observed strong quenching by acrylamide in aqueous solution (Ksv of 29.2 M−1) and robust protection of quenching by the addition of lipid vesicles (Ksv of 11.2 M−1; Figure 2F), confirming that PcTx1 can interact with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PcTx1 can interact with membranes.
source: When these experiments were performed with PcTx1, we again observed strong quenching by acrylamide in aqueous solution (Ksv of 29.2 M−1) and robust protection of quenching by the addition of lipid vesicles (Ksv of 11.2 M−1; Figure 2F), confirming that PcTx1 can interact with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by acrylamide quenching experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: GxTx-1E has a Kdx value of (1.1 ± 0.2) × 10^7 determined from acrylamide dequenching experiments.
source: When the increase in maximal fluorescence intensity was plotted against the available lipid concentration and a partition function fit to the data, a Kdx value of (1.1 ± 0.2) × 107 was obtained for GxTx-1E, in reasonable agreement with the mole fraction partition coefficient for the toxin determined using blue-shifts in Trp fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis from Figure 3C.

claim: PcTx1 has a Kdx value of (4.3 ± 0.6) × 10^6 from acrylamide dequenching experiments.
source: In the case of PcTx1, we obtained a value of (4.3 ± 0.6) × 106, demonstrating that PcTx1 interacts strongly with membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis from Figure 3D.

claim: The solvent accessible surface area for the hydrophobic surface of PcTx1 is 380 Å^2.
source: For example, the solvent accessible surface area for the hydrophobic surface of PcTx1 is 380 Å2, which compares with a value of 703 Å2 for GxTx-1E.
evidence: This is a calculated value from structural analysis.

claim: The solvent accessible surface area for the hydrophobic surface of GxTx-1E is 703 Å^2.
source: For example, the solvent accessible surface area for the hydrophobic surface of PcTx1 is 380 Å2, which compares with a value of 703 Å2 for GxTx-1E.
evidence: This is a calculated value from structural analysis.

claim: GxTx-1E exhibits strong quenching by brominated lipids similar to what has been reported for other voltage-sensor toxins.
source: When we performed quenching experiments with these three brominated lipids and GxTx-1E, we observed strong quenching that is similar to what has been reported previously for other voltage-sensor toxins (Figure 3E) (Phillips et al., 2005; Swartz, 2007; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014), confirming an intimate interaction of the toxin with the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous work.

claim: GxTx-1E has an intimate interaction with the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
source: When we performed quenching experiments with these three brominated lipids and GxTx-1E, we observed strong quenching that is similar to what has been reported previously for other voltage-sensor toxins (Figure 3E) (Phillips et al., 2005; Swartz, 2007; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014), confirming an intimate interaction of the toxin with the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the brominated lipid quenching data.

claim: PcTx1 exhibits only very weak quenching by brominated lipids.
source: Interestingly, when we undertook similar experiments with PcTx1, we observed only very weak quenching by brominated lipids, again with only relatively small differences between the three lipids (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The weak quenching of PcTx1 by brominated lipids indicates that this toxin interacts considerably more superficially with membranes compared to voltage-sensor toxins.
source: The measurable quenching observed for PcTx1 confirms that this toxin interacts with membranes, however, the much weaker quenching when compared to voltage-sensor toxins indicates that this toxin interacts considerably more superficially with membranes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the brominated lipid quenching data comparing PcTx1 to voltage-sensor toxins.

claim: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 bound to ASIC shows that the toxin interacts primarily with residues on one face of thumb helix-5.
source: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 bound to ASIC shows that the toxin interacts primarily with residues on one face of thumb helix-5, with an interface comprised of both hydrophobic and polar residue interactions (Figure 1G) (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and reference to Figure 1G.

claim: The PcTx1-ASIC interface is comprised of both hydrophobic and polar residue interactions.
source: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 bound to ASIC shows that the toxin interacts primarily with residues on one face of thumb helix-5, with an interface comprised of both hydrophobic and polar residue interactions (Figure 1G) (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and reference to Figure 1G.

claim: PcTx1 contains an Arg finger motif composed of R26, R27 and R28 that is required for activation of ASIC.
source: PcTx1 also contains an Arg finger motif composed of R26, R27 and R28 that is required for activation of ASIC through interactions with channel residues situated in a crevice between subunits.
evidence: This is a structural and functional observation from the crystal structure and previous studies.

claim: The S3b helix within the voltage-sensing domains of Kv channels contains the most influential determinants of voltage-sensor toxin binding.
source: In the case of voltage-sensor toxins such as hanatoxin and GxTx-1E, the S3b helix within the voltage-sensing domains of Kv channels contains the most influential determinants of toxin binding, and these also involve a combination of hydrophobic and polar residue interactions (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997b; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 2000, 2001; Alabi et al., 2007; Milescu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: PcTx1 has nM affinity for ASIC1a.
source: PcTx1 has nM affinity for ASIC1a (Chen et al., 2006; Dawson et al., 2012), but even at very high concentrations (5 µM) has no effect on the Kv2.1 channel (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data.

claim: PcTx1 at 5 µM has no effect on the Kv2.1 channel.
source: PcTx1 has nM affinity for ASIC1a (Chen et al., 2006; Dawson et al., 2012), but even at very high concentrations (5 µM) has no effect on the Kv2.1 channel (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The voltage-sensor paddle can be transplanted between different channels that contain S1–S4 domains without disrupting voltage sensor function.
source: Previous chimera studies have shown that the voltage-sensor paddle, a helix-turn-helix motif comprised of S3b and S4 helices, can be transplanted between different channels that contain S1–S4 domains without disrupting voltage sensor function (Alabi et al., 2007; Bosmans et al., 2008, 2011b; Kalia and Swartz, 2013), making us optimistic that helix-5 transfer might be possible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous chimera studies.

claim: All five Kv2.1-ASIC1a chimeras gave rise to robust voltage-activated K+ currents.
source: All five chimeras gave rise to robust voltage-activated K+ currents and displayed voltage-activation relations that were shifted to more depolarized voltages when compared to the wild-type Kv2.1 channel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G), consistent with disruption of the interactions between S3b and S4 helices that have been shown to stabilize voltage sensors in an activated state (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: The voltage-activation relations of the five Kv2.1-ASIC1a chimeras were shifted to more depolarized voltages when compared to the wild-type Kv2.1 channel.
source: All five chimeras gave rise to robust voltage-activated K+ currents and displayed voltage-activation relations that were shifted to more depolarized voltages when compared to the wild-type Kv2.1 channel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G), consistent with disruption of the interactions between S3b and S4 helices that have been shown to stabilize voltage sensors in an activated state (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: High concentrations of PcTx1 had no discernible effect on the activity of any of the five Kv2.1-ASIC1a chimeras.
source: Although these relatively radical chimeras were all functional, extracellular application of high concentrations of PcTx1 had no discernible effect on the activity of any of them (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: GxTx-1E alanine mutants were generated for 29 out of 36 residues using solid phase chemical synthesis.
source: We generated Ala mutants for 29 out of 36 residues of GxTx-1E (excluding one native Ala and 6 Cys residues) using solid phase chemical synthesis, and successfully folded all but one in mg quantities (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and results.

claim: GxTx-1E mutants exhibited a wide range of different phenotypes, from small changes in affinity to almost 400-fold weakening of toxin affinity for Kv2.1.
source: We obtained estimates of the apparent affinity for each mutant, and observed a wide range of different phenotypes, from small changes in affinity to almost 400-fold weakening of toxin affinity for Kv2.1 (Figure 4D; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: A well-defined surface of GxTx-1E was identified where mutations having dramatic effects on the apparent affinity of the toxin cluster together.
source: When perturbation energies (∆∆G values) for each mutant were mapped onto the NMR structure of GxTx-1E, a well-defined surface of the toxin was identified where mutations having dramatic effects on the apparent affinity of the toxin cluster together (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data mapped onto the structure in Figure 5A.

claim: The GxTx-1E binding surface contains many aromatic residues (F7, W8, W9, Y22 and W28), one aliphatic hydrophobic residue (L30) and several polar residues (K10, K15, S25, K27 and N32).
source: This surface contains many aromatic residues (F7, W8, W9, Y22 and W28), one aliphatic hydrophobic residue (L30) and several polar residues (K10, K15, S25, K27 and N32).
evidence: This is a description of the residues identified in the binding surface from mutagenesis data.

claim: The mutations producing the most dramatic perturbations on the GxTx-1E binding surface were for mutations of aromatic residues.
source: The mutations producing the most dramatic perturbations on this surface were for mutations of aromatic residues, whereas those for the polar residues were relatively modest (Figure 5A; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: The three Trp mutants of GxTx-1E (W8A, W9A, W28A) obtained Kx values that were within a factor of two for the wild-type toxin.
source: Even though the apparent affinities of these mutants for Kv2.1 ranged from 26 to almost 200-fold lower (Figure 4D; Table 1), we obtained Kx values that were within a factor of two for the wild-type toxin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each of the three Trp mutants of GxTx-1E exhibited robust quenching by brominated lipids.
source: We also measured quenching of the three Trp mutants by brominated lipids and found that each exhibited robust quenching (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The blue-shifts observed with membrane partitioning vary for the three Trp mutants of GxTx-1E.
source: It is notable that the blue-shifts observed with membrane partitioning vary for the three Trp mutants, as does the extent of quenching by brominated lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the three Trp residues reside in non-equivalent environments within the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The three Trp residues in GxTx-1E reside in non-equivalent environments within the membrane.
source: It is notable that the blue-shifts observed with membrane partitioning vary for the three Trp mutants, as does the extent of quenching by brominated lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the three Trp residues reside in non-equivalent environments within the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the varying spectroscopic properties of the Trp mutants.

claim: There is extensive overlap between the active surfaces of PcTx1 and GxTx-1E responsible for binding to ASIC1a and Kv2.1 channels.
source: The comparison reveals an extensive overlap between the active surfaces of the two toxins responsible for binding to ASIC1a and Kv2.1 channels, indicating that the two classes of toxins use related surfaces for interacting with helices within structurally unrelated ion channel proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of mutagenesis data (Figure 5A) and structural analysis (Figure 5B, C).

claim: The two classes of tarantula toxins use related surfaces for interacting with helices within structurally unrelated ion channel proteins.
source: The comparison reveals an extensive overlap between the active surfaces of the two toxins responsible for binding to ASIC1a and Kv2.1 channels, indicating that the two classes of toxins use related surfaces for interacting with helices within structurally unrelated ion channel proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of binding surfaces.

claim: Both classes of tarantula toxins interact with membranes.
source: The results of our experiments demonstrate that both classes of toxins interact with membranes (Figures 2, 3), a finding that is consistent with the amphipathic character evident in the solution structures of these toxins (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The interaction of PcTx1 with membranes is different than what has been observed for voltage-sensor toxins.
source: However, our results also show that the interaction of PcTx1 with membranes is different than what has been observed for voltage-sensor toxins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the spectroscopic properties of PcTx1 and voltage-sensor toxins.

claim: Trp residues on PcTx1 exhibit only very small blue shifts when interacting with membranes.
source: Fluorescence spectroscopy results show that Trp residues on PcTx1 exhibit only very small blue shifts when interacting with membranes (Figure 2), and that the Trp fluorescence of the toxin is only weakly quenched by bromine atoms on the acyl chains of lipids (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Trp fluorescence of PcTx1 is only weakly quenched by bromine atoms on the acyl chains of lipids.
source: Fluorescence spectroscopy results show that Trp residues on PcTx1 exhibit only very small blue shifts when interacting with membranes (Figure 2), and that the Trp fluorescence of the toxin is only weakly quenched by bromine atoms on the acyl chains of lipids (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Voltage-sensor toxins typically exhibit strong blue shifts in Trp fluorescence and this is robustly quenched by brominated lipids.
source: In contrast, voltage-sensor toxins typically exhibit strong blue shifts in Trp fluorescence and this is robustly quenched by brominated lipids (Figures 2, 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The stark differences observed for PcTx1 demonstrate that tarantula toxins of similar structure do not necessarily have similar membrane interacting properties.
source: Although these properties have been consistently observed for other voltage-sensor toxins (Jung et al., 2005; Phillips et al., 2005; Milescu et al., 2007, 2009; Swartz, 2007; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014), the stark differences observed here for PcTx1 demonstrate that tarantula toxins of similar structure do not necessarily have similar membrane interacting properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the membrane interaction properties of PcTx1 and voltage-sensor toxins.

claim: The membrane interactions of voltage-sensor toxins are unique in how far they can penetrate the lipid bilayer.
source: The membrane interactions of voltage-sensor toxins are unique in how far they can penetrate the lipid bilayer, further supporting the idea that this class of toxins interacts with voltage sensors within the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the depth-dependent quenching experiments.

claim: The PcTx1 binding site on ASIC is located about 45 Å above from the lipid bilayer.
source: Although a complex structure of PcTx1 and ASIC shows that the PcTx1 binding site is located about 45 Å above from the lipid bilayer, superficial adsorption of the toxin to the membrane would be predicted to enhance the rate of complex formation due to a reduction in dimensionality of diffusion (Axelrod and Wang, 1994).
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure.

claim: Superficial adsorption of PcTx1 to the membrane would be predicted to enhance the rate of complex formation due to a reduction in dimensionality of diffusion.
source: Although a complex structure of PcTx1 and ASIC shows that the PcTx1 binding site is located about 45 Å above from the lipid bilayer, superficial adsorption of the toxin to the membrane would be predicted to enhance the rate of complex formation due to a reduction in dimensionality of diffusion (Axelrod and Wang, 1994).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on biophysical principles and cited literature.

claim: Membrane interactions have been reported for charybdotoxin, a strongly cationic scorpion toxin that blocks the external pore of some potassium channels.
source: Interestingly, membrane interactions have also been reported for charybdotoxin (Ben-Tal et al., 1997), a strongly cationic scorpion toxin that blocks the external pore of some potassium channels (Miller, 1995; Banerjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The interaction of charybdotoxin with membranes is heavily influenced by electrostatic interactions.
source: The interaction of charybdotoxin with membranes is heavily influenced by electrostatic interactions, suggesting that the toxin interacts relatively superficially, similar to what we observed with PcTx1.
evidence: This is an interpretation from previous studies on charybdotoxin.

claim: The inhibitor cystine knot (ICK) fold is found in many toxins and is thought to provide a structurally stable scaffold for presentation of surfaces to bind to receptors and ion channel proteins.
source: The inhibitor cystine knot (ICK) fold is found in many toxins and is thought to provide a structurally stable scaffold for presentation of surfaces to bind to receptors and ion channel proteins (Pallaghy et al., 1994; Norton and Pallaghy, 1998), and in principle many unique surfaces on these toxins could be used for this purpose.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GxTx-1E uses a surface to bind to the S3b helix within voltage sensors that is similar to that which PcTx1 uses to bind to helix-5 in ASIC.
source: However, our results show that GxTx-1E uses a surface to bind to the S3b helix within voltage sensors that is similar to that which PcTx1 uses to bind to helix-5 in ASIC (Figure 5), even though the former binds within a membrane environment and the latter in aqueous solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data and structural comparisons shown in Figure 5.

claim: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 in complex with ASIC shows that the toxin clamps onto a solvent-exposed lateral surface of helix-5.
source: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 in complex with ASIC shows that the toxin clamps onto a solvent-exposed lateral surface of helix-5 (Figure 1) (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012), using a somewhat concave surface of the toxin formed by residues in loop 1 and loop 3, including both hydrophobic (W7, W24, F30, and P35) and polar residues (K8, K25, R26, S29 and T37).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and reference to Figure 1.

claim: PcTx1 uses a somewhat concave surface formed by residues in loop 1 and loop 3 to bind helix-5, including both hydrophobic (W7, W24, F30, and P35) and polar residues (K8, K25, R26, S29 and T37).
source: The X-ray structure of PcTx1 in complex with ASIC shows that the toxin clamps onto a solvent-exposed lateral surface of helix-5 (Figure 1) (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012), using a somewhat concave surface of the toxin formed by residues in loop 1 and loop 3, including both hydrophobic (W7, W24, F30, and P35) and polar residues (K8, K25, R26, S29 and T37).
evidence: This is a description of the binding interface from the crystal structure.

claim: The equivalent surface of GxTx-1E is formed by residues in loop 1 and loop 3 containing hydrophobic (F7, W8, W9, Y22, W28 and L30) and polar residues (K10, K15, S25, K27 and N32) where mutations weaken the apparent affinity of the toxin.
source: The equivalent surface of GxTx-1E is also formed by residues in loop 1 and loop 3 (Figure 5), which contain a similar variety of hydrophobic (F7, W8, W9, Y22, W28 and L30) and polar residues (K10, K15, S25, K27 and N32) where mutations weaken the apparent affinity of the toxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The binding surface of GxTx-1E is similar to that identified on SGTx1.
source: This surface is also similar to that identified on SGTx1 (Wang et al., 2004; Milescu et al., 2007), a tarantula toxin related to hanatoxin and GxTx-1E that inhibits the Kv2.1 channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies on SGTx1.

claim: Residues having disproportionately large effects on the apparent affinity of SGTx1 compared to the strength of membrane partitioning cluster together on a surface similar to what was identified for GxTx-1E.
source: Although the apparent affinity of the most critical mutants on SGTx1 could not be accurately determined because the affinity of the toxin is quite low (Wang et al., 2004), residues having disproportionately large effects on the apparent affinity of the toxin compared to the strength of membrane partitioning cluster together on a surface that is similar to what we identified here for GxTx-1E (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Milescu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: This face of the ICK fold forms a shape complement for α-helices that may be exploited by many other peptide ligands.
source: Given the similar binding faces for α-helices on 3 peptide toxins that share little commonality besides an tri-cystine scaffold, we suggest that this face of the ICK fold forms a shape complement (Jones, 2012) for α-helices that may be exploited by many other peptide ligands.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed similarity in binding surfaces across multiple toxins.

claim: The preferred model of GxTx-1E bound to the activated/open Kv1.2/Kv2.1 paddle chimera positions the largest number of critical residues in GxTx-1E where they can interact with residues in the S3b helix.
source: Although all three models position critical residues on GxTx-1E where they can interact with the S3b helix, our preferred model (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1E, 2E) positions the largest number of critical residues in GxTx-1E where they can interact with residues in the S3b helix.
evidence: This is a description of the computational modeling results shown in Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: In the preferred model, the toxin interacts with many of the most critical residues within the S3b helix that have been identified using mutagenesis.
source: In addition, in this model the toxin interacts with many of the most critical residues within the S3b helix that have been identified using mutagenesis (Figure 6) (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997b; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 2000, 2001; Milescu et al., 2009), with a placement of the toxin within the membrane that is compatible with the depth of partitioning inferred using spectroscopic and neutron diffraction approaches (Phillips et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2010; Mihailescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational model shown in Figure 6 and citations to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: Voltage-sensor toxins like GxTx-1E bind tighter to and stabilize the resting/closed state of Kv channels.
source: Voltage-sensor toxins like GxTx-1E bind tighter to and stabilize the resting/closed state of Kv channels, however, they can remain bound when the voltage sensors activate and the channel opens (Phillips et al., 2005; Tilley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Voltage-sensor toxins can remain bound when the voltage sensors activate and the channel opens.
source: Voltage-sensor toxins like GxTx-1E bind tighter to and stabilize the resting/closed state of Kv channels, however, they can remain bound when the voltage sensors activate and the channel opens (Phillips et al., 2005; Tilley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: All GxTx-1E peptides were synthesized with norleucine (Nle) in place of Met35 to avoid oxidation of the toxin.
source: All the GxTx1E peptides were synthesized with norleucine (Nle) in place of Met35 to avoid oxidation of the toxin.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: GxTx-1E inhibits opening of the Kv2.1 and engineered Shaker Kv channels with relatively high affinity.
source: GxTx-1E inhibits opening of the Kv2.1 and engineered Shaker Kv channels with relatively high affinity (Herrington et al., 2006; Milescu et al., 2009; Schmalhofer et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010; Milescu et al., 2013; Tilley et al., 2014), it can be produced using solid-phase peptide synthesis, efficiently folded in vitro (Lee et al., 2010; Tilley et al., 2014) (see 'Materials and methods') and its solution structure has been solved (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: GxTx-1E can be produced using solid-phase peptide synthesis and efficiently folded in vitro.
source: GxTx-1E inhibits opening of the Kv2.1 and engineered Shaker Kv channels with relatively high affinity (Herrington et al., 2006; Milescu et al., 2009; Schmalhofer et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010; Milescu et al., 2013; Tilley et al., 2014), it can be produced using solid-phase peptide synthesis, efficiently folded in vitro (Lee et al., 2010; Tilley et al., 2014) (see 'Materials and methods') and its solution structure has been solved (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and the methods section.

claim: The solution structure of GxTx-1E has been solved.
source: GxTx-1E inhibits opening of the Kv2.1 and engineered Shaker Kv channels with relatively high affinity (Herrington et al., 2006; Milescu et al., 2009; Schmalhofer et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010; Milescu et al., 2013; Tilley et al., 2014), it can be produced using solid-phase peptide synthesis, efficiently folded in vitro (Lee et al., 2010; Tilley et al., 2014) (see 'Materials and methods') and its solution structure has been solved (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the structure determination study.
